{{Short description|American physical chemist (1933–2024)}}
'''Kenneth B. Eisenthal''' (March 23, 1933 – March 3, 2024) was an American [[physical chemist]].<ref name=bio>{{cite journal
   | author = The Eisenthal Group
   | title = Biography of Kenneth B. Eisenthal
   | journal = Journal of Physical Chemistry C
   | volume = 111
   | number = 25
   | year = 2007
   | pages = 8699–8702
   | doi = 10.1021/jp079508f| doi-access = free
   }}</ref>

==Life and career==
Eisenthal was born in [[New York City]] on March 23, 1933. He received a B.S. in chemistry from [[Brooklyn College]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Flygare Memorial Lecture 2009-10 - Kenneth B. Eisenthal|website=Department of Chemistry, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/flygare-memorial-lecturer-2009-10-kenneth-b-eisenthal}}</ref> He graduated from [[Harvard University]] with an M.A. in physics and a Ph.D. in chemical physics. His doctoral thesis supervisor was [[Marshall Fixman]]. As a postdoc, Eisenthal worked at UCLA ([[University of California, Los Angeles]]), where he gained experience in [[molecular spectroscopy]] in the research group of [[Mostafa El-Sayed]]. After his stay at UCLA, Eisenthal briefly worked at [[The Aerospace Corporation]] and then at the [[IBM Almaden Research Center]], where he did research in the Chemical Physics Group. The application of lasers in chemistry (laser chemistry) became his main field of work. The development of the [[picosecond]] laser in the late 1960s created new possibilities for measuring molecular relaxation processes. Eisenthal made important contributions to the then new field of picosecond-[[laser spectroscopy]]. In 1975 he moved to [[Columbia University]], as the holder of a professorship ("Mark Hyman Professor of Chemistry"). At Columbia University he did fundamental research on [[Solvated electron|free electron]]s in water, the photochemistry of [[carbenes]], and other photochemical processes (photoisomerization), before his research activities focused on the application of lasers to investigation of the equilibrium and dynamic properties of molecules at liquid interfaces and at solid interfaces.<ref name=bio/>

Eisenthal was the author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles. His co-authors include [[Nicholas Turro]]. Eisenthal was a Guggenheim Fellow for the academic year 1984–1985.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kenneth B. Eisenthal|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/kenneth-b-eisenthal/}}</ref> In 1986 he was elected a fellow of the American Physical Society. He received in 1998 the {{ill|ACS Award in Surface Chemistry|de}} from the [[American Chemical Society]], in 2016 the {{ill|Joel Henry Hildebrand Award|de}}, and in 2014 the {{ill|ACS Award in Colloid Chemistry|de}}. In 2000 he was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/kenneth-b-eisenthal-cxcgno/ | title = Member Directory: Kenneth B. Eisenthal | website = National Academy of Sciences (nasonline.org)}}</ref>

Eisenthal died on March 3, 2024, at the age of 90.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kenneth Eisenthal |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/nytimes/name/kenneth-eisenthal-obituary?id=54602250 |website=Legacy |access-date=19 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Professor Kenneth B. Eisenthal (1933 – 2024) |url=https://www.chem.columbia.edu/news/professor-kenneth-b-eisenthal-1933-2024 |website=Columbia University Department of Chemistry |access-date=20 December 2024 |date=6 March 2024}}</ref>
